newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil stock market looks beyond re-election.
newsitem.headline: Brazil stock market looks beyond re-election.

text.p: With profits taken on re-election, investors now want to see government progress on economic reforms before pumping fresh capital into Brazilian stocks, analysts said.
"Approval of re-election was very positive, but now the market will begin thinking about future problems," said Sidney Chamey, head of research for Fator Securities in Brazil.

Profit-takers swooped down today on Brazil's bolsas -- which were up strongly in recent weeks as investors anticipated initial passage of a re-election amendment -- after Congress' lower house approved the bill Tuesday night.
The amendment faces a second vote in the Chamber of Deputies and two votes in the Senate.

But with the first and largest hurdle cleared Tuesday, foreign investors are now looking for signs of progress on fiscal, pension and administrative reforms, privatizations and new legislation for oil, telecoms and other sectors.
"I don't think we'll see any significant new inflows of capital in the short term as a result of re-election," said Walter Mendes, head of Schroder Investment Management Ltd's Brazil office.
"But in the medium term, if we see progress on privatization and reforms, we'll see some more capital coming in," he added.

Analysts said foreigners, now sitting out the spate of mostly local profit-taking, might step in to take positions if prices continued sliding because the medium and long-term outlook for Brazilian stocks is good.

Investors favor the idea of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso running for an unprecedented second term in 1998 because it holds the promise of political continuity and progress on getting Congress to back economic reforms.
Analysts said Tuesday's government victory was "very positive" for long-term investors, who can now look forward to the possibility of six more years of political and economic stability.
"The market does not like doubt. If you don't have re-election, the market will begin to speculate earlier about who the next president is going to be," Mendes said.
The short-term impact on the market, however, will be mild because investors anticipated approval and prices and volumes already reflected optimism surrounding re-election, they said.
As a result, the focus of investors now will shift to whether Cardoso can harness the political clout and momentum gained from re-election to further his economic program, analysts said.

"The current moment in Brazilian political development could become the start of a broad political reform process...and the resumption of the agenda for economic reforms," ING Barings said in a special re-election report.

Failure to do so, it added, would reinforce the impression that Brazil's leaders lack political maturity and that "policy makers will continue to muddle through with unstable political support, barely transparent negotiations and other problems."
